title: Hypertext Transfer Protocol Version 2 (HTTP/2)

hero.subtitle: Binary framing, multiplexing, and header compression for a faster Web

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
HTTP/2 is a major revision of the HTTP protocol that dramatically improves performance while maintaining full backward compatibility with HTTP/1.1 semantics. The same methods, status codes, and headers are used; only the transport mechanism changes.

HTTP/2 evolved from Google's experimental SPDY protocol. It addresses HTTP/1.1's head-of-line blocking problem by introducing binary framing and multiplexed streams.
sections.eli5: HTTP is how browsers ask for web pages. HTTP/2 asks the same questions but packs them into a smarter shipping container so many can travel together.

sections.title: Overview
sections.content:
HTTP/2 replaces HTTP/1.1's text-based protocol with a binary framing layer that enables significant performance improvements:

Binary Protocol
Unlike HTTP/1.1's text-based format, HTTP/2 uses a compact binary framing. This is more efficient to parse and less error-prone, though no longer human-readable on the wire.
Single TCP Connection
HTTP/2 uses a single TCP connection per origin, eliminating the overhead of multiple connections while achieving better throughput through multiplexing.
sections.eli5: Instead of writing messages in words, HTTP/2 uses compact codes that computers read quickly, and it sends everything through one pipe instead of opening many.

sections.title: Streams and Multiplexing
sections.content:
Multiplexing is the core innovation of HTTP/2. Multiple requests and responses can be in flight simultaneously on a single connection:

Streams
Each request/response pair occupies an independent stream identified by a unique integer. Streams are logically independent, so a slow response on one stream does not block others at the HTTP layer.
Frames
Streams are composed of frames — the smallest unit of communication. Frame types include HEADERS, DATA, SETTINGS, PUSH_PROMISE, PING, and others.
Stream Priority
Clients can assign priority to streams, indicating which resources are most important. Servers use this to allocate bandwidth between competing streams.

While HTTP/2 eliminates HTTP-level head-of-line blocking, TCP-level head-of-line blocking remains. A single lost TCP packet blocks all multiplexed streams. This motivated the development of HTTP/3 over QUIC.
sections.eli5: Imagine sending several letters in one envelope, torn into pieces with a number on each piece. The receiver puts each pile back together, so a slow letter does not hold up the others.

sections.title: Frame Format
sections.content:
Every frame starts with a fixed 9-byte header, shown in the figure above, followed by a payload whose size is given in the Length field. Some of the frame types defined by this document:

0x0DATA — Carries request/response body data
0x1HEADERS — Carries HTTP header fields
0x2PRIORITY — Stream priority information
0x3RST_STREAM — Terminate a single stream
0x4SETTINGS — Connection configuration parameters
0x5PUSH_PROMISE — Server push notification
sections.eli5: Every piece begins with the same small label: how long it is, what kind it is, a few switches, and which letter it belongs to.

sections.title: HPACK
sections.content:
HPACK is the header compression algorithm used by HTTP/2, defined in RFC 7541. It dramatically reduces header overhead:

Static Table
A predefined table of 61 common header field/value pairs (e.g., :method: GET, :status: 200). These can be referenced by a single index byte.
Dynamic Table
A connection-specific table built up during the session. Previously sent headers are added to this table and can be referenced by index in subsequent requests.
Huffman Coding
String literals can be Huffman-encoded using a static Huffman code optimized for HTTP header values.

HPACK is particularly effective for HTTP because headers are highly repetitive across requests. After the first request, subsequent requests often require only a few bytes of header data.
sections.eli5: Browsers say the same things over and over, like "I am Chrome". HPACK makes both sides remember them, so next time a tiny nickname is enough.

sections.title: Server Push
sections.content:
HTTP/2 allows servers to proactively send resources to the client before they are requested:

PUSH_PROMISE
The server sends a PUSH_PROMISE frame indicating it will push a resource. The client can reject the push with RST_STREAM if it already has the resource cached.
Use Case
When a client requests an HTML page, the server can proactively push the CSS and JavaScript files it knows will be needed, saving a round trip.

Server push has seen limited adoption in practice, and Chrome has removed support for it. Other techniques such as preload hints are now commonly used instead.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the shop can guess what you will want next and hand it over early. You can say no thanks if you already have it.

sections.title: Flow Control
sections.content:
HTTP/2 implements its own flow control mechanism at the stream and connection level, independent of TCP flow control:

Initial Window Size65,535 bytes (can be changed via SETTINGS)
ScopePer-stream and per-connection
WINDOW_UPDATEFrame type used to increase the flow control window

Flow control ensures that a single stream cannot monopolize the connection and that receivers are not overwhelmed with data they cannot process.
sections.eli5: A receiver can say "slow down, my hands are full" so one big download cannot hog the pipe or overwhelm the person on the other end.

references.text: Peon, R. and H. Ruellan, "HPACK: Header Compression for HTTP/2", RFC 7541, May 2015.
Fielding, R., et al., "Hypertext Transfer Protocol -- HTTP/1.1", RFC 2616, June 1999.

subtitle: Binary framing, multiplexing, and header compression for a faster Web.
summary: HTTP/2 keeps the meaning of HTTP (the same methods, status codes and headers) but changes how it is carried. Messages are split into binary frames that belong to numbered streams, so many requests and responses can share one TCP connection at once, and headers are compressed with HPACK.

eli5.summary: Instead of one long checkout line, HTTP/2 lets many shoppers' items go down the same belt mixed together, each item labelled with who it belongs to.

questions: what is the http/2 frame format

tldr.problem: HTTP/1.1 needs many parallel connections or serialized requests, and repeats large text headers on every request.
tldr.mechanism: Split each message into binary frames tagged with a stream identifier, interleave many streams on one TCP connection, and compress headers with HPACK.
tldr.outcome: Faster page loads with fewer connections, but one lost TCP packet still stalls every stream, which led to HTTP/3 over QUIC.

today: HTTP/2 is supported by major browsers and web servers and is typically negotiated inside TLS. Server push saw little use and Chrome has since removed support for it. RFC 7540 has been obsoleted by RFC 9113, which keeps the design but deprecates the stream-priority scheme described here. HTTP/3 (RFC 9114) carries the same semantics over QUIC to avoid TCP head-of-line blocking.

implementations.note: Major web servers, CDNs and browsers support HTTP/2 over TLS.

layers.label: HTTP semantics
layers.detail: Methods, headers, status codes (unchanged from HTTP/1.1)

layers.label: TLS 1.2 or later
layers.detail: Used by browsers in practice; cleartext h2c is also defined

viz.caption: two requests interleaved on one connection

messages.label: HEADERS, stream 3 (GET /b)
messages.note: Sent without waiting for a reply to stream 1.

messages.label: HEADERS + DATA, stream 3
messages.note: The reply to /b can finish first.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Length of the frame payload in bytes, not counting the 9-byte header. Must not exceed 16,384 unless the receiver set a larger SETTINGS_MAX_FRAME_SIZE.

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: Frame type, such as 0x0 DATA or 0x1 HEADERS. Unknown types must be ignored and discarded.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: Boolean flags specific to the frame type. Unassigned flags are sent as 0 and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: Reserved bit. Must be 0 when sending and ignored when receiving.

fields.name: Stream Identifier
fields.desc: The stream this frame belongs to. 0x0 means the connection as a whole.
